longForm.title: The Strait of Salamis: How Greece Turned Back the Persian Empire
longForm.excerpt: In September 480 BC, the Athenian fleet lured the Persian navy into a narrow strait and destroyed it in a single day. The victory halted Xerxes' invasion and reshaped the Mediterranean world.
paragraphs: The Persian fleet entered the Strait of Salamis on a dawn morning in September 480 BC. Xerxes had come to conquer Greece, had ferried perhaps 300,000 men across the Hellespont, broken the pass at Thermopylae, and marched his army into Attica. The Greeks had no choice but to fight at sea, in waters they knew better than the Persians did. Themistocles of Athens had already made the decision: the narrow strait would be his killing ground.

The Persian fleet numbered over 1,000 ships by most accounts—triremes and lighter vessels, crewed by Phoenicians and Egyptians, commanded by men who had never fought in Greek waters. The Athenian force under Themistocles held perhaps 300 triremes, many freshly built, their crews barely trained. The arithmetic looked catastrophic. But Themistocles had seen something the Persian commanders had not: in confined water, numbers become a liability. A thousand ships cannot maneuver. They cannot support each other. They pile into each other.

At dawn on the date later fixed as 29 September 480 BC—though ancient sources disagree on the exact day—the Persian fleet began to advance into the strait. The Athenians held position near the shore. Herodotus records that Xerxes watched from a throne on the hillside above the water, attended by his generals and scribes, who recorded the battle as it happened. What he witnessed was the systematic destruction of his naval advantage.

The Athenian triremes rowed forward in a controlled line. They struck the Persian ships at an angle, ramming the hull below the waterline with their bronze-sheathed prows. A trireme struck hard could splinter. The Phoenician crews, crowded into narrow hulls, had no room to maneuver and few trained marines for boarding combat. As Persian ships sank, they blocked the advance of ships behind them. The strait became a coffin.

The fighting lasted one day. By afternoon, the Athenian crews—exhausted, drenched in spray and blood, their ships taking on water from ramming damage—held the strait. The Persian fleet had lost perhaps 200 ships and thousands of crew. Greek losses were severe but recoverable. More important: the invasion had broken. Xerxes, watching from the hill, realized the arithmetic had reversed. He withdrew to Asia Minor, leaving his general Mardonius behind with an army that would be defeated the following summer at Plataea.

What made Salamis decisive was not the size of the engagement but its strategic consequence. The Persian Empire had come to conquer Greece with a force that seemed irresistible. It failed at sea. Themistocles' insight—that a Persian advantage in numbers became a disadvantage in confined water—proved correct, and it held. The Greeks had no navy capable of challenging Persian power in open ocean. But in the shallows of home waters, where tight formations mattered more than numbers, they could fight on equal terms.

The cultural impact was immediate. The Athenians had held. The myth of Persian invincibility, carefully cultivated since the reign of Darius, had a crack in it. Salamis did not end the Persian threat to Greece—that would come at Plataea and Mycale—but it proved that the threat could be challenged. The Mediterranean powers that would rise after Persia's eventual withdrawal—eventually, Athens itself—could trace a line back to a single dawn in 480 BC, when a navy that should have been overwhelmed held a strait instead.

The aftermath was complicated. Themistocles' victory made him a power in Athens, but his growing influence alarmed the city's other leaders. Within a decade he would be ostracized and eventually exiled. The Athenian navy that had saved Greece would, within 70 years, drag Athens into the Peloponnesian War and toward eventual defeat. But in the moment after Salamis, none of that mattered. Greece had survived. The Persian fleet would not return to Greek waters in force again.

Later historians would debate what would have happened had Themistocles lost the strait. Would the Persian army have marched south and crushed the remaining Greek cities in open field battle? Probably yes. Would Greek civilization as it developed—democratic Athens, the philosophical tradition that would flow from it—have survived a Persian conquest? The question has no answer. But it is the right question to ask. One day in one strait changed the trajectory of the Western world.

shortForm.title: Poltava: When Peter the Great Broke Swedish Power
shortForm.excerpt: At Poltava in 1709, Peter the Great's Russian army destroyed Charles XII of Sweden's invasion force. The victory marked the end of Swedish dominance in Eastern Europe and the rise of Russia.
paragraphs: Charles XII of Sweden was 27 years old and had never lost a battle. He had fought the Poles, the Saxons, the Danes—all of them had been broken by the Swedish Army. In 1708, he crossed into Russia with perhaps 45,000 men, expecting the same rapid destruction. Instead, the Russians burned everything in his path. The Cossack allies Charles had relied on switched sides. By the time the Swedish army reached Poltava, it was starving, worn down by 6,000 miles of march through hostile territory.

Peter the Great, commanding from the Russian side, had learned from his earlier defeats. At Narva in 1700, his army had been shattered by the same Charles XII. Now, 9 years later, Peter's infantry and artillery had improved dramatically. He had built a fortified camp at Poltava. On 8 July 1709, Charles XII, desperate and outnumbered, attacked. The Russians held the line. The Swedish cavalry charges, which had won every battle before this one, broke against Russian guns.

By afternoon, Swedish ranks had collapsed. Charles XII escaped to Ottoman territory with a remnant of his army. Russia had lost perhaps 6,000 men; Sweden had lost nearly 20,000—dead, wounded, or captured. The Swedish Empire would not recover. Peter became the dominant power in Eastern Europe, and Russia replaced Sweden as the region's military arbiter. One battle had reordered the continent.

sources.label: Voltaire, The History of the Russian Empire Under Peter the Great

onThisDay.headline: Battle of the Coral Sea: First Naval Battle Fought Entirely by Aircraft
onThisDay.summary: The Battle of the Coral Sea (May 7-8, 1942) was fought entirely by carrier-based aircraft—neither fleet saw the other. American and Australian forces stopped Japanese expansion toward Australia, marking the strategic turning point in the Pacific War.
